title: Prezent
theme: Želim, želiš, and želi show that who hangs on the end of the doing-word.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you learn the full now-map for doing-words you already say in pieces. Book 1 gave you želim, volim, and imam as ready chunks. Those endings are the same family on almost every everyday verb. English hangs I, you, and they in front and leaves the verb mostly still. Bosnian hangs the who on the end of the doing-word. This chapter is only the present map. Aspect and past wait for later.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because the lines I want, you want, and they want keep the word want almost untouched. A tiny s on wants is the whole show for he and she. Bosnian changes the end for nearly every who, so želim is I want, želiš is you want, and želi is he or she wants. The little words ja and ti are optional once the ending is clear. Schools call this prezent, which means the present. You can keep saying the now-map and still be right.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. That m on želim is the I mark. Emir can say Želiš kahvu when he means you want coffee, and Amira can say Želi kahvu when she means he or she wants coffee. Same verb stem. Different who. Today you stop treating želim as a frozen tourist phrase and start seeing the whole row.
knownLine.speaker: Ana

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: Most everyday verbs take a short who-ending in the present. Ja takes m, so želim and radim. Ti takes š, so želiš and radiš. On, ona, and ono often take a bare ending, so želi and radi. Mi takes mo, and vi takes te. They often take e, as in žele and rade, and some families take ju instead, as in piju from piti. Željeti and raditi are honest samples from the same town words you already know. You can keep ja and ti off the page when the ending already says who, and you learn the row first before watching for a few pests that refuse the cheat sheet.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Two everyday verbs refuse the neat row, and you should memorize them early because Book 1 already uses both habits. Ići means to go, but the present is idem, ideš, ide, idemo, idete, idu, not a fake ićim. Biti means to be, and the short present is sam, si, je, smo, ste, su. Saying ja biti or ja ićim invents a tourist form. Do not argue with idem and sam. Just file them beside the regular map.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to keep saying ja želim as if ja does the real work. The m already marks I. Bosnian often drops ja, ti, and even on when the ending is clear. The other trap is to treat every Book 1 chunk as a frozen postcard. Volim, imam, and govorim are the same who-map as želim. If you invent English-style I want without the Bosnian ending, you erase the whole system this chapter teaches.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester hung who-marks on doing-words the way Bosnian still does. Singan could change for I, you, and they. Later English wore most of that off. You kept a scrap in am, is, and are, and a tiny s on wants. You speak the later version.

Bosnian never fired the who-marks on željeti. The present endings are leftover person marks from the same old habit. Schools call the tidy chart prezent. Today you only need the living row on coffee, work, and going. Tomorrow is whether the action is finished, which is a different system on the same verbs.

Biti pest. Short sam is the everyday present.

items.prompt: Someone says Ja želim every time. What is the soft fix?
options: Add ja after every verb ending.
Drop ja when m already marks I.
Switch to English word order only.
items.explanation: The ending carries who. Ja is optional.

items.prompt: Polite you want coffee. Which form?
items.explanation: Te covers you-all and polite you.
Oni take -e on željeti: žele. -ju is a later preview on some verbs like piti, not today’s željeti map.

questions.question: What is today’s system?
options: Filing he, she, and leftover piles
questions.explanation: Piles and jobs were earlier. Today is prezent.

questions.question: The m on želim marks which who?
options: nobody. Ja does all the work.
questions.explanation: M is the I ending. Ja is optional.

questions.question: Why is Idem kući correct, not Ićim kući?
options: Because ići is a pest in the present
Because kući forces a bare ending
questions.explanation: Ići uses idem, ideš, ide. Memorize it.

questions.question: Ovdje sam uses which pest verb?
questions.explanation: Biti has the short present sam, si, je, smo, ste, su.

questions.question: What comes next after the present map?
options: Seven noun jobs on one page
Aspect. Eat versus eat up on two verbs
questions.explanation: Chapter 9 is vid. Same coffee, new system.

next.body: You now have the present who-map behind želim, radim, and the Book 1 chunks, plus the pests idem and sam. Chapter 9 is why Bosnian often needs two verbs for one English verb, eat versus eat up. The who-endings stay. The finish-line changes.
